question: A 50-year-old man with a chronic bronchitis who was admitted for a pneumonic episode with a blood culture positive for Streptococcus pneumoniae, with a CMI at penicillin of 0.0125 mg / l. Treatment with 2 million penicillin is started every 4 hours. On the fifth day it continues with a fever of 38ºC. Which of the following decisions do you think is right?

options.opa: I would change the treatment to ceftriaxone because of its greater efficacy.
options.opb: I would add a quinolone to the treatment.
options.opc: I would switch to amoxicillin / clavulanic acid.
options.opd: It would rule out the presence of a pleural empyema.
options.ope: I would continue with the same treatment, assuming that it is simply a problem of time.

enhanced_information: In a 50-year-old man with chronic bronchitis and a pneumonic episode caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae with a CMI at penicillin of 0.0125 mg/l, continuing to have a fever on the fifth day raises concerns. Considering the options, it would be appropriate to rule out the presence of pleural empyema before making any changes to the antibiotic treatment.
analysis: In this case, the patient is a 50-year-old man with chronic bronchitis and a pneumonic episode caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae. Despite being on penicillin treatment, he continues to have a fever on the fifth day. Given this scenario, it is crucial to rule out the presence of pleural empyema before considering changing the antibiotic regimen. Pleural empyema can be a complication of pneumonia and may require specific management. Therefore, the priority should be to investigate this possibility before making any treatment adjustments.
